thread.title: Double Down: Top Deals In Today's Tech

author: Harry Sauers
title: Double Down: Top Deals In Today's Tech
text:
Being a young, risk-on investor, I do not shy away from high-growth tech stocks despite sometimes lofty valuations. I believe the sector has a long way to go, when working with an ample time horizon. I am willing to wait years for a thesis to play out, and when prices decline (like in Alibaba (NYSE: BABA )), I will happily buy more. This strategy is not suitable for everyone, but has led to outsize risk-adjusted returns over time for myself and others.
Thanks to macro headwinds, widespread skepticism, and the current bear market in FAANG stocks, many names in tech are trading at quite reasonable valuations. I will evaluate my top picks of Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Alibaba, and Hercules Capital (NASDAQ: HTGC ) (a small-cap BDC). Though JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM ) is a financial services firm, they spend nearly $10B annually on technology and are looked on as the frontrunner in Wall Street innovation – I believe they deserve inclusion in this list.
These names have taken a serious beating in the past several months, and now are available at firesale prices to those who are willing to buy and hold with conviction.
Apple:
For perhaps the best-known (and best-managed) company in the world, Apple shares don’t command much of a premium these days. The stock trades at a meager 14 times earnings, which is less than half that of the broader large-cap tech sector. Though investors should consider Apple’s ability to grow earnings, these fears are grossly overblown – Mr. Tim Cook oversaw 29% earnings growth over the past year, and the unique pricing power of both the iPhone and Mac lines allows for further margin expansion. No other company is able to manufacture excellent devices that sell at nearly triple the cost of their parts . This fact alone is something that ought to command a premium to the industry more along the lines of stalwart companies like Procter and Gamble if not higher, rather than priced for failure and sluggishness – and I say this as the proud owner of a Google Pixel phone.
Apple’s strong balance sheet allows it to finance debt at mere basis points above the U.S. government and provides downside protection. Their low debt also offers the opportunity to access far more leverage than their current $115B (should management deem it beneficial). At the time of this writing, Apple’s share price is roughly $172 a share, down more than 25% from the all-time high.
I believe Apple’s intrinsic value is well north of today’s price, or somewhere in the mid-twenties times earnings – upwards of $220-280 a share, implying around 40% upside. Apple’s 10-year trailing PE of 25 implies a similar upside. This represents a rare opportunity to own one of America’s finest businesses at a steep discount to its intrinsic value.
Intel:
Intel is another firm that has taken a beating, though is in a more cyclical market due to its heavy dependence on supplier pricing and consumer demand. It remained relatively insulated from the crypto boom that hurt companies like AMD and NVIDIA, but now trades just shy of 20% down from their all-time high. This indicates another potential bargain. Investors should be aware of the cyclical and secular risks in the semiconductor industry, which generally stem from supply and competition.
Fortunately, Intel also enjoys strong pricing power for their chips and are considered the industry standard in the tech world – I personally refuse to use other processors on my machines – and is able to maintain a healthy operating margin of 32%. Intel has invested heavily into excellence in technology and has been rewarded handsomely for it, arguably now the backbone of American technology infrastructure. It remains largely insulated from competitors (only AMD is even worth mentioning – and AMD’s operating margin is a meager 7.56%).
This effective duopoly indicates a low threat of emerging competition, and with Intel controlling nearly 80% of the CPU market, it is clearly here to stay -- and as investors, we ought to love high barriers to entry. I recently purchased shares of Intel at around $47 and plan to buy more as capital becomes available.
Alibaba:
Perhaps one of the most controversial names in tech, Alibaba shares appear severely undervalued for the “Amazon of China.” Events such as founder and CEO Jack Ma stepping down , the trade war, and concerns over Chinese accounting have blown the stock down as low as $133 a share in October. This demonstrates a clear emotional overreaction by the market to a few negative events that have borne little real impact on the company.
Alibaba recently reported a blowout singles day and excellent earnings per share, which is only set to be beaten further when Q4 earnings are reported. Alibaba has a history of beating expectations , both in earnings and in accomplishments, and this year is no different. Its cloud segment is growing as well, and in time may become a viable competitor to Amazon’s unit. Evidently, none of these events are being priced in, while all the negatives of the aggregate Chinese market have been. Both the iShares China ETF ( MCHI ) and Alibaba are sitting at a 29% decline from their 52-week highs, which is telling. Do you think Alibaba deserves to be priced based more on what the Chinese market is like, or based on the business’s fundamentals?
Though BABA’s P/E ratio of around 40 is (by traditional measures) not cheap, it is more than justified in the rapid earnings growth. It is poised for excellent long-term success and ought to be assigned a multiple much closer to Amazon’s 92 times trailing earnings , rather than priced for failures that are almost unimaginable to occur. Valuation compression may have found a floor for this excellent business.
The biggest risk to the long thesis, is regulatory – though not from the United States. China’s authoritarian regime has warmed up to consumer markets, but failures of state-run enterprises, lack of credit, and “hidden debt” could force Chinese officials to levy higher taxes or even seize assets, neither of which would be unprecedented. However, such a move would effectively destroy any willingness the West has to invest in or provide credit to China – not something President Xi Jinping seems eager to do.
Overall, BABA appears to be a very compelling play that may be on the uptrend now. I have doubled down on my own investment and find the underlying business to be stronger than ever. Earnings growth trends alone imply 8-32% upside, while valuation expansion adds at least 20% if we peg fair value around 50x earnings.
This valuation is somewhat lofty but deserved given Alibaba's excellent diversification, conservative balance sheet, and immense potential for growth across all markets and segments. Volatility doesn't appear to be over, but when trade and interest rate tensions become clear, we can expect to see a corresponding rise in prices.
Hercules Capital:
Though not directly a technology company, Hercules Capital provides exposure to early-stage tech companies under the management of Mr. Manuel Henriquez. It is considered a BDC. An investment in HTGC comes with a yield of about 10%, as of today. HTGC invests in senior secured loans to venture-backed technology startups and is well-positioned in these for rising interest rates, as most is financed at floating rates. Conservative use of its own access to debt is another upside, allowing management flexibility in their investments moving forward. Nearly all debt has been financed at fixed rates well into the future, and interest is well-covered.
The dividend is similarly safe, with HTGC actually distributing a special dividend of $0.02/share the past quarter to shareholders. This indicates that management has confidence in their ability to keep the dividend safe and is comfortable with debt levels.
Shares are up about 2% for the year.The company provides compelling total return and exposure to high-risk, high-growth private businesses with limited downside through debt instruments.
Though shares don't appear dramatically undervalued, continued dividend reinvestment coupled with modest share price appreciation offers a strong total return thesis and exposure to a unique market segment. I hold shares personally and have been quite happy with the performance and added diversification.
JPMorgan:
JPMorgan is one of the most well-known financial services firms on Wall Street, for its rich history and investment banking services. However, it is also one of the most high-tech banks out there, investing nearly $10B into technology each year , which represents 16% of its annual expenses. For this reason, JPMorgan warrants a spot in my tech picks, since their advances in automation and artificial intelligence are practically unrivaled by large-cap financials.
It's no secret that JPM's stock has taken a beating lately, down 11% from previous highs. The bank stock may have room to fall, but big names – including Warren Buffett – have been buying up both JPM and the financial sector due to their ridiculously low valuations. JPM trades at just 13x earnings and a 3% yield, while the financial sector ( XLF ) trades at 16x earnings and 1.8% yield.
Not only is JPMorgan undervalued relative to the sector, but it is one of few firms that isn't under fire for serious consumer exploitation (not to mention Jamie Dimon's excellence). However, JPM's Shiller PE implies an undervaluation of roughly 35% (19.5 Shiller, 13 today).
JPM is possibly best-run large financial company in the world, and this is simply not reflected in its current valuations. The stock isn't seen as “sexy” or high-tech, but excellence in management and covert investments into IT plus a fantastic dividend growth rate make this stock a great long-term play at deep value prices.
In Conclusion :
These names represent value plays into a high-growth sector and are among the world's most respected businesses. Despite some secular headwinds, fears that have been depressing prices are either severely overblown or not even real. Time will reward those who are willing to wait for the market to return to sanity. I have long positions in all of the above companies except for Apple, which I own indirectly via VGT, XLK, and BRK.B and rate each one a “strong buy” on excellent fundamentals and irrational pricing.
Thanks for reading. Please let me hear your thoughts on these picks and feel free to mention any other names you feel are compelling in today's market.
Disclosure: I am/we are long INTC, BABA, HTGC, JPM, BRK.B.
